narration.text: Freeways are multi-lane, controlled-access, divided highways with no stops and no cross traffic, built for long trips with less fatigue and more safety. To use them well, you need to know their special rules. In this lesson you will learn how to keep pace with traffic, where slower vehicles belong, why weaving between lanes is dangerous, how to change lanes properly, and what to do if your car breaks down, including the distress signals that bring help and how to reach the Alabama State Troopers by phone. Keep right if you are slower than the flow.

Safe freeway driving means keeping pace with traffic and staying alert, and vehicles moving slower than the normal flow must keep to the right. Weaving from lane to lane is dangerous; pick a lane moving at the pace you want and stay in it. When you must change lanes to pass or exit, check traffic carefully and signal well before you move. These habits make you predictable. Drivers around you can plan around a car that stays in its lane and signals early, but not around one that darts back and forth. Keep right if you are slower than the flow.

narration.text: In a freeway breakdown, park completely off the traveled lanes and stay with the vehicle if you possibly can. The distress signals are an open trunk, a raised hood if weather allows, and a white cloth tied to a door handle or antenna, and an officer who sees them will help. To reach Alabama State Troopers about highway emergencies, crashes or drunk drivers, dial star H P, which is star forty-seven, free from a cell phone. Parking on the freeway is not allowed except in an emergency. Keep right if you are slower than the flow. Park on the freeway only in an emergency.

The distress signals work because officers patrolling the freeway recognize them. An open trunk, a raised hood if weather allows, and a white cloth tied to a door handle or antenna tell an officer that you need help. A phone call to the State Troopers at star H P, or star forty-seven, is another way to get help for a breakdown, a crash you witness, or a drunk driver you see. Meanwhile, stay with your vehicle if you possibly can, parked completely off the traveled lanes, rather than walking along the freeway. Keep right if you are slower than the flow.

Here is the trap. Some drivers pull onto the freeway shoulder to make a call, check a map or rest. Parking on the freeway is not allowed except in an emergency. A breakdown is an emergency, and then you park completely off the traveled lanes, stay with the vehicle if you can, and use the distress signals. But for a phone call or a map check, get off at the next exit instead. Freeway shoulders sit beside fast traffic, so stopping there without a real emergency puts you and others at risk. Keep right if you are slower than the flow. Park on the freeway only in an emergency.

Knowing interchange types, such as the diamond where left turns come after you exit, helps you find the right ramp.

narration.text: This lesson covers getting onto a freeway and the interchanges that connect highways. You will learn how entrance ramps and acceleration lanes work, how to merge, who yields when merging, what to do on a ramp with a YIELD sign and no acceleration lane, and the four common interchange types: directional, cloverleaf, diamond and trumpet. Merging is one of the trickiest parts of freeway driving, because you must reach the speed of traffic and find a gap at the same time, so a clear routine helps. Use the acceleration lane to match speed. The entering driver yields.

Entrance ramps are short one-way ramps that lead to an acceleration lane, where you speed up to match through traffic if possible. From the acceleration lane, watch for a gap, signal, and merge smoothly into traffic. Do not stop completely in the acceleration lane unless it is absolutely necessary, because a stopped car there has to enter freeway traffic from a standstill, which is far more dangerous. The acceleration lane exists so that you can join the freeway at about the same speed as the cars already on it. Use the acceleration lane to match speed.

Freeway drivers should leave room for merging traffic, but an entering driver must yield if they do not. On an entrance ramp with a YIELD sign and no acceleration lane, entering drivers obey the sign and stop if needed instead of forcing their way in. So courtesy from freeway drivers is expected, but the legal duty to yield rests with the driver entering. Plan your merge so that you can fit into a gap, and be ready to slow or stop at a yield-controlled ramp until there is a safe opening in traffic. Use the acceleration lane to match speed.

An interchange joins two highways at different levels with separate connecting roads, so vehicles can cross, enter or leave without interfering with others. Four common types are directional, cloverleaf, diamond and trumpet. A directional interchange serves heavy traffic moving between only two legs, with other movements handled by ordinary diamond-type ramps. A cloverleaf uses loop connections for turns on and off the freeway from four directions and removes left-turn and cross-traffic conflicts. A diamond has four ramps, with left turns made after you leave the freeway, and a trumpet gives access where another road meets the freeway in a T.

Here is the trap. At a diamond interchange, drivers sometimes look for a way to turn left directly from the freeway. A diamond interchange lets you enter and leave with the flow on four ramps, and any left turn comes only after you are off the freeway, never on it. By contrast, a cloverleaf uses loop connections so that left turns and cross-traffic conflicts are removed altogether. So if you need to go left at a diamond, take the exit ramp first, then make your left turn on the crossing road. Use the acceleration lane to match speed. The entering driver yields.

narration.text: Getting off the freeway at the right place requires advance planning and close attention to the signs. In this lesson you will learn how to prepare for your exit, where to slow down, what to expect at the end of the exit ramp, and what to do if you miss your exit. These rules prevent some of the most dangerous freeway moves: cutting across lanes at the last moment, braking hard in the through lanes, and stopping, backing up or turning around after realizing you have gone past the exit you wanted. Slow in the deceleration lane, not the through lane.

To exit, signal, enter the deceleration lane and slow there, never slowing suddenly on the freeway itself, and be ready to yield or stop at the end of the ramp where it meets the intersecting road. The deceleration lane is the mirror image of the acceleration lane: one is for speeding up to join traffic, the other is for slowing down after you leave it. Keep your freeway speed until you are in it. Slow in the deceleration lane, not the through lane. Never stop or back up on the freeway.

narration.text: If you miss your exit, do not stop, back up or turn around; go on to the next exit and come back. Stopping or backing up on a freeway puts you directly in the path of fast traffic, and turning around is not possible safely. A few extra miles to the next exit is a small price compared with the danger of any of those moves. If you know your route ahead of time and watch the signs, missing an exit becomes much less likely in the first place, which is why planning matters. Slow in the deceleration lane, not the through lane. Never stop or back up on the freeway.

Here is the trap. Drivers sometimes brake in the through lane as they approach their exit, slowing traffic behind them. The manual says to signal, enter the deceleration lane and slow there, never slowing suddenly on the freeway itself. Once you are on the ramp, be ready to yield or stop where it meets the intersecting road. So the order is: move to the proper lane early, signal, move into the deceleration lane at freeway speed, and only then slow down. Braking early in the through lane is the mistake to avoid. Slow in the deceleration lane, not the through lane.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: how should you prepare for an exit you see coming up? Decide on your answer first. The answer is to plan early, watch the signs, and move into the proper lane well ahead of time. Then signal, enter the deceleration lane and slow there, never suddenly on the freeway itself, and be ready to yield or stop at the end of the ramp. If you still miss the exit, do not stop, back up or turn around; go on to the next exit and come back to the one you missed. Slow in the deceleration lane, not the through lane. Never stop or back up on the freeway.

To wrap up, getting off the freeway starts with planning: watch the signs and move into the proper lane well ahead of your exit. Signal, enter the deceleration lane and slow down there, not suddenly in the through lanes, and be ready to yield or stop at the end of the ramp. If you miss your exit, never stop, back up or turn around on the freeway. Go on to the next exit and come back. These simple steps keep your exit smooth and keep you out of the path of the fast traffic behind you. Slow in the deceleration lane, not the through lane. Never stop or back up on the freeway.

narration.text: You cannot be a safe driver unless your vehicle is properly equipped and mechanically sound, and Alabama law sets the safety equipment required. In this lesson you will learn the rules for brakes, mufflers and exhaust systems, windshield wipers, rear view mirrors and lights, including the distances your mirrors and lights must meet. You will also see that flashing both turn signals as hazard lights is permitted. Knowing these rules helps you keep your car legal and spot problems before they cause a crash or a ticket. Mirrors two hundred, lights five hundred, high beams three fifty.

Every automobile needs two separate ways of applying the brakes: a regular foot brake and a parking brake. Every vehicle needs a working muffler that stops excessive or unusual noise, and muffler cutouts, bypasses and similar devices are forbidden. The exhaust system must not leak carbon monoxide into the vehicle and should be checked periodically. So the brakes give you a backup way to stop and hold the car, the muffler keeps noise down, and a sound exhaust system protects you and your passengers from dangerous fumes. Mirrors two hundred, lights five hundred, high beams three fifty.

Lights seen from five hundred feet.

narration.text: Any motor vehicle with a windshield must have wipers in good working order. All vehicles must have rear view mirrors that let the driver see two hundred feet behind. Required lighting includes a minimum of two white headlights, one or more red taillights, a brake light, and a light over the rear license plate. All lights must be visible from at least five hundred feet, and the high beam must light objects at least three hundred fifty feet away and stay properly aimed. Flashing both turn signals to warn of a hazard is permitted. Mirrors two hundred, lights five hundred, high beams three fifty.

A vehicle in poor condition can fail at the worst moment, which is why the law sets equipment rules and why you cannot be a safe driver unless your vehicle is properly equipped and mechanically sound. A brake that does not hold, a mirror that does not show far enough, a light others cannot see, or an exhaust leak can each turn an ordinary trip into an emergency. Checking these items regularly, and fixing them promptly, keeps your car legal and gives you the best chance of avoiding a crash. Mirrors two hundred, lights five hundred, high beams three fifty.

lines.text: Lights five hundred; high beams three fifty.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Three distances appear in the equipment rules, and they are easy to mix up. Rear view mirrors must show two hundred feet behind, while every light must be visible from five hundred feet and high beams must reach three hundred fifty feet. A question might offer five hundred feet for the mirror or two hundred feet for the lights. Keep each number with its item: two hundred for mirrors looking back, five hundred for being seen, and three hundred fifty for how far your high beams light the road ahead. Mirrors two hundred, lights five hundred, high beams three fifty.

Here is a quick check: may you turn on both turn signals at once to warn others of a problem with your vehicle? Decide on your answer first. The answer is yes. The law permits flashing both turn signals, or another pair of lights, at the same time to warn of a vehicle hazard. That is useful in a breakdown, along with parking completely off the traveled lanes and using distress signals on a freeway. Your other lights must still meet their rules, visible from at least five hundred feet. Mirrors two hundred, lights five hundred, high beams three fifty.

To close, a safe driver needs a properly equipped, mechanically sound vehicle. Every automobile needs a foot brake and a parking brake. Every vehicle needs a working muffler without cutouts or bypasses, and an exhaust that does not leak carbon monoxide inside. Vehicles with windshields need working wipers, and mirrors must show two hundred feet behind. Required lights include two white headlights, red taillights, a brake light and a plate light, all visible from five hundred feet, with high beams reaching three hundred fifty feet. Flashing both turn signals to warn of a hazard is permitted.

narration.text: This lesson covers three more pieces of required equipment and how to use them. You will learn how safety belts prevent the second collisions that cause many crash deaths, why small children need special restraints, the rules for horns and sirens, and how to care for your tires, including the tread depth that makes a tire illegal. Each of these is simple, but together they make a big difference in whether a crash is survivable and whether your car can stop and steer when you need it to. Safety belts prevent second collisions. Never mix tire types.

In crashes, steering assemblies cause thirty percent of fatal injuries, and hitting the windshield, its frame or the dash causes another forty percent; these are second collisions that safety belts can prevent. Children under six years old need special child and infant restraints to protect them from serious injury or death. Traffic crashes are the leading killer of children, and child and infant restraints keep small children from becoming flying missiles in a crash. So belts for adults and proper restraints for children prevent the most common causes of crash deaths.

Every motor vehicle needs a working horn, and bells, sirens or exhaust whistles are allowed only on emergency vehicles. Use the horn only to give a warning reasonably needed for safety, never to announce arrival or call passengers, because needless use can lead to arrest. You can use it to warn children, bicyclists, pedestrians or drivers you are passing. So the horn is a safety tool, not a doorbell. Using it for anything other than a needed warning is not just impolite; it can bring legal trouble. Safety belts prevent second collisions. Never mix tire types.

Buy tires rated to carry your car's weight, check pressure often, never drive on under-inflated tires, and have uneven wear checked for wheel or alignment problems. A tire is illegal once its tread is less than one sixteenth of an inch deep. Avoid jack-rabbit starts and screeching stops unless truly necessary, go easy on corners and rough roads, let tires cool on long hot trips, and check the spare now and then. Never use different types of tires, and ask your dealer before mixing types between front and back. Safety belts prevent second collisions.
